paper_a.title: Visualizing Data using t-SNE (van der Maaten & Hinton, 2008)

paper_b.title: UMAP: Uniform Manifold Approximation and Projection for Dimension Reduction (McInnes, Healy, Melville, 2018)

metadata.description: t-SNE and UMAP are the two dominant nonlinear dimensionality reduction methods for visualization. Both construct a high-dimensional neighbor graph and optimize a low-dimensional embedding to preserve neighborhood structure. t-SNE uses Gaussian similarities + KL divergence with a Student-t kernel. UMAP uses fuzzy simplicial sets + cross-entropy with a similar heavy-tailed kernel. UMAP is faster, preserves more global structure, and has a theoretical grounding in topology, while t-SNE pioneered the approach and popularized the Student-t kernel idea.

matches.explanation: Both construct a weighted neighbor graph in high-dimensional space. t-SNE: Gaussian kernel with per-point bandwidth $\sigma_i$ set by perplexity, then symmetrize. UMAP: exponential kernel with local distance normalization ($\rho_i$ and $\sigma_i$ set to achieve $\log_2(k)$ effective neighbors), then symmetrize via fuzzy union. Both normalize distances locally to handle varying data density. The fuzzy simplicial set interpretation is UMAP's theoretical contribution.

Both use a local bandwidth parameter controlling the effective neighborhood size. t-SNE: perplexity (log-effective-neighbors, typically 5-50). UMAP: number of nearest neighbors $k$ (typically 15). Both perform binary search for bandwidth. Functionally equivalent mechanisms for adapting to local data density.

Both use a heavy-tailed kernel in the embedding space. t-SNE: Student-t with 1 DOF (Cauchy): $q_{ij} \propto (1 + \|y_i - y_j\|^2)^{-1}$. UMAP: parametric family $v_{ij} = (1 + a\|y_i - y_j\|^{2b})^{-1}$ which closely approximates the Student-t when $a \approx b \approx 1$. Both solve the crowding problem by allowing dissimilar points to be placed far apart cheaply.

The key algorithmic difference. t-SNE: minimizes KL divergence $\sum p_{ij} \log(p_{ij}/q_{ij})$, which only has an attractive force (large $p$ with small $q$ is penalized, but not the reverse). Global normalization of $q_{ij}$ provides implicit repulsion. UMAP: minimizes cross-entropy $\sum [w \log(w/v) + (1-w)\log((1-w)/(1-v))]$, which has both attractive and explicit repulsive terms. The repulsive term is why UMAP preserves more global structure.

Both optimize via gradient-based methods but with different approaches. t-SNE: gradient descent on all pairs with early exaggeration and momentum. UMAP: SGD with edge sampling + negative sampling (similar to word2vec training), which is much more scalable. UMAP's optimization is $O(n)$ per epoch vs. t-SNE's $O(n^2)$ (or $O(n \log n)$ with Barnes-Hut).
t-SNE's explicit identification and discussion of the 'crowding problem' is a conceptual contribution. UMAP inherits the solution (heavy-tailed kernel) without emphasizing this specific motivation.

Both discuss computational complexity. t-SNE: $O(n^2)$ naive, $O(n \log n)$ with Barnes-Hut. UMAP: empirically $O(n^{1.14})$, significantly faster. UMAP's speed advantage is one of its main practical selling points.

UMAP's theoretical grounding in category theory, fuzzy simplicial sets, and Riemannian geometry is unique. t-SNE has no such theoretical framework; it is motivated by practical considerations (crowding problem, KL divergence properties).

UMAP explicitly compares to t-SNE and shows that its cross-entropy objective relates closely to t-SNE's KL divergence when restricted to the attractive component, but adds the repulsive term for global structure preservation.
